Vary a trend effect along the trend's axis

Source: R/lv_axis.R
lv_axis.Rd

Use lv_axis() in a trend_formula in any position that takes a factor variable, to give each latent factor its own effect. In a model with no latent factors it gives each series its own effect.

Usage

lv_axis()

Value

NULL (invisibly). The function exists solely as a formula sentinel.

Details


trend_formula = ~ s(elev, by = lv_axis()) + AR(n_lv = 2)
trend_formula = ~ temp:lv_axis() + AR(n_lv = 2)
trend_formula = ~ (1 + temp | lv_axis()) + AR()
trend_formula = ~ s(temp, lv_axis(), bs = "fs") + AR()

With n_lv set on the trend constructor, each factor k = 1, ..., n_lv takes its own effect. The effect of a covariate on series s is the sum over factors of the loading Z[s, k] times the effect on factor k. This is constrained ordination, the model jsdgam() fits. Every term of such a trend_formula is then evaluated once per factor and time. Each covariate must take one value per time.

With no n_lv, each series takes its own effect on the latent state.

The series column itself is not supported in a trend_formula term. Write lv_axis() for an effect that differs along the trend's axis. An effect of the series on the observations belongs in formula. by = trend is deprecated and is treated as by = lv_axis().

What each form estimates

With no latent factors, lv_axis() is each series:

  • ~ x:lv_axis() gives a slope of x per series.

  • ~ lv_axis() gives a level per series.

  • ~ (1 + x | lv_axis()) gives levels and slopes that are partially pooled across series.

  • ~ s(x, by = lv_axis()) gives a smooth of x per series, and ~ s(x, lv_axis(), bs = "fs") gives smooths that share a smoothness penalty.

With n_lv latent factors, each of these is estimated once per factor. The coefficient of one factor has no scale of its own. The loadings and the factor effects trade scale. The data identify their product. conditional_effects() and predict() report that product, the effect of the covariate on each series, and conditional_effects() draws a panel per series. When every lv_axis() term is a slope or a level, cmdstanr::summary() reports the per-factor coefficients in the basis of the identified loadings Z_tilde.

See also

jsdgam() fits per-factor effects across species. conditional_effects.mvgam() plots the effect on each series. The dynamic factor vignette fits factor models. The JSDM article fits per-factor trait and covariate effects.

Other trend models: LLT(), PW(), RW(), ZMVN(), list_trend_types()

Examples

# `lv_axis()` marks a term in a formula. Called by itself it
# returns NULL.
lv_axis()

# \dontrun{
# Three series whose seasonal effect differs: 1, 0.5 and -1
set.seed(1)
dat <- sim_mvgam(family = gaussian(), n_series = 3L,
                 n_timepoints = 60L)$data_train
dat$season <- sin(2 * pi * dat$time / 12)
dat$y <- dat$y + c(1, 0.5, -1)[as.integer(dat$series)] * dat$season

# One seasonal slope per series
mod <- mvgam(
  formula       = y ~ 1,
  trend_formula = ~ season:lv_axis() + AR(p = 1),
  data          = dat,
  family        = gaussian(),
  chains        = 2,
  silent        = 2
)
#> Warning: 33 of 2000 (2.0%) transitions ended with a divergence.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.
summary(mod)

# With two latent factors, each factor takes a seasonal slope. The
# loadings carry the two slopes to the three series. The prior
# table lists one coefficient per factor. A smooth takes the same
# marker: `s(season, by = lv_axis())`
get_prior(
  mvgam_formula(y ~ 1,
                trend_formula = ~ season:lv_axis() + AR(p = 1, n_lv = 2)),
  data   = dat,
  family = gaussian()
)
